questions.q:
A wall shelf has the shape of quadrilateral ABCD, with angle A = angle B = 90 degrees at the two corners along the wall edge AB.
(a) Using AB as a transversal, explain why AD is parallel to BC.
(b) The carpenter says, 'Two right angles are enough, so the shelf is a rectangle.' Give a set of angles for C and D that proves him wrong, and say why they are possible.
questions.a: (a) AB is a transversal to AD and BC, and the angles on the same side of it add to 90 + 90 = 180 degrees, so AD is parallel to BC. (b) For example angle C = 70 degrees and angle D = 110 degrees. The four angles add to 90 + 90 + 70 + 110 = 360 degrees, so such a quadrilateral can exist, but it does not have all four angles 90 degrees, so it is not a rectangle. (Any pair C, D adding to 180 other than 90 and 90 is correct.)
s: Part (a): angles on the same side of transversal AB add to 180, so AD is parallel to BC
Part (b): a valid pair such as 70 and 110 degrees with the 360 degree check, so not a rectangle

questions.a: (a) Angle K is 90 degrees, so angle MKN = 90 - 34 = 56 degrees. (b) OK = OL (half of equal diagonals), so angle OLK = 34 degrees and angle KOL = 180 - 68 = 112 degrees. The acute angle between the diagonals is 180 - 112 = 68 degrees.
s: Part (a): 56 degrees from the 90 degree corner
Part (b): uses OK = OL to get angle KOL = 112 degrees and the acute angle 68 degrees

questions.q: Ravi joins two 10 cm sticks at their midpoints so that the angle between them is only 25 degrees, and runs a thread round the ends. He says, 'This is still a rectangle, even though the sticks are nowhere near 90 degrees to each other.' Is Ravi right? Support your answer by finding a corner angle of the thread figure.
questions.a: Yes, Ravi is right. The half-sticks are all 5 cm, so the four triangles at the joint are isosceles. With apex 25 degrees the base angles are (180 - 25) / 2 = 77.5 degrees; with apex 155 degrees the base angles are (180 - 155) / 2 = 12.5 degrees. Each corner is made of one angle of each kind: 77.5 + 12.5 = 90 degrees. Equal diagonals that bisect each other always give a rectangle, whatever the angle between them.
s: Gives the verdict that Ravi is right
Finds the base angles 77.5 and 12.5 degrees from the isosceles triangles
Adds them to 90 degrees and states the angle between the diagonals does not matter

questions.q:
A mason marking out a rectangular room has only a measuring tape, no set-square.
(a) Which definition of a rectangle can he use, and what must he measure?
(b) Why is checking that both pairs of opposite sides are equal not enough?
questions.a: (a) A rectangle is a quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal and bisect each other, so he measures both diagonals (equal) and checks that they cross at their midpoints. (b) A parallelogram that is not a rectangle, for example one with sides 4 m, 5 m, 4 m, 5 m and an angle of 30 degrees, also has equal opposite sides, so equal opposite sides do not force right angles.
s: Part (a): uses equal diagonals that bisect each other and says what to measure
Part (b): gives a parallelogram with equal opposite sides that is not a rectangle

questions.q: A frame-maker says her quadrilateral ABCD has all four angles equal to 90 degrees, with AB = 40 cm, BC = 25 cm, CD = 38 cm and DA = 25 cm. Show that such a quadrilateral cannot exist.
questions.a: Join BD. In triangles BAD and DCB, angle A = angle C = 90 degrees and BD is common. Angle ABD + angle DBC = 90 and, in triangle BCD, angle BDC + angle DBC = 90, so angle ABD = angle BDC. By AAS, triangle BAD is congruent to triangle DCB, so AB = CD. But AB = 40 cm and CD = 38 cm, so the four right angles and these sides cannot go together.
s: Sets up triangles BAD and DCB with the right angles and the common side
Shows angle ABD = angle BDC and concludes congruence by AAS
Deduces AB = CD, which contradicts 40 cm and 38 cm

questions.q:
In rectangle WXYZ the diagonals meet at O, and angle XOY is 3 times angle WOX.
(a) Find angle WOX and angle XOY.
(b) Find angle OWX.
(c) Find angle OXY and check that angle WXY comes to 90 degrees.
questions.a: (a) Angles WOX and XOY form a straight angle, so 4 x angle WOX = 180, giving angle WOX = 45 degrees and angle XOY = 135 degrees. (b) OW = OX, so angle OWX = (180 - 45) / 2 = 67.5 degrees. (c) OX = OY, so angle OXY = (180 - 135) / 2 = 22.5 degrees. Angle WXY = angle OXW + angle OXY = 67.5 + 22.5 = 90 degrees.
s: Part (a): 45 and 135 degrees from the straight angle
Part (b): 67.5 degrees from the isosceles triangle OWX
Part (c): 22.5 degrees and the check 67.5 + 22.5 = 90

questions.q:
Some farmers mark the base of a house with two equal ropes pegged so that they cross at their midpoints; the four rope ends are the corners of the base. A farmer in Jharkhand uses two ropes, each 14 m long. The owner wants the longer walls to be such that each rope makes an angle of 35 degrees with a longer wall at its corner.
(a) At what angle must the ropes cross, measured on the side of a shorter wall?
(b) Find the angle each rope makes with a shorter wall, and check the corner angle.
(c) The helper has run short of time and offers two quick ways: way 1, two 14 m ropes pegged to cross at the 6 m mark of one and the 7 m mark of the other; way 2, a 14 m rope and a 12 m rope, each pegged at its own midpoint. Which way, if either, gives a rectangular base? Justify both.
questions.a: (a) The triangle on a longer wall has two 7 m sides and base angles of 35 degrees, so its angle at the crossing is 180 - 70 = 110 degrees. The angle on the side of a shorter wall is 180 - 110 = 70 degrees. (b) That triangle is isosceles with apex 70 degrees, so each rope makes (180 - 70) / 2 = 55 degrees with a shorter wall; the corner is 35 + 55 = 90 degrees. (c) Neither. In way 1 the ropes are equal but the 14 m rope crossed at its 6 m mark is cut into 6 m and 8 m, so the diagonals do not bisect each other; the diagonals of every rectangle do. In way 2 the ropes bisect each other but are unequal (14 m and 12 m), while the diagonals of a rectangle are always equal; this gives only a parallelogram. Both conditions, equal and bisecting, are needed together.
s: Part (a): finds 110 degrees on the longer wall and hence 70 degrees
Part (b): finds 55 degrees and checks 35 + 55 = 90
Part (c): rejects both ways, way 1 because the diagonals do not bisect each other and way 2 because they are unequal

questions.q:
A student draws quadrilateral ABCD with diagonals AC and BD meeting at O. She records: OA = OB = OC = OD = 9 cm, angle OAB = 40 degrees and angle OBC = 45 degrees.
(a) Explain why ABCD must be a rectangle.
(b) Using triangle AOB, find angle OBA and angle AOB.
(c) Hence find what angle OBC must be, and show that her record cannot be fully right.
(d) Suppose instead the 45 degree reading is right and the 40 degree reading is wrong. Find angle OAB and angle AOB in that case.
(e) Her teacher measures angle AOD and gets 80 degrees. Which of her two angle readings was wrong? Justify.
questions.a: (a) AC = 9 + 9 = 18 cm and BD = 9 + 9 = 18 cm, so the diagonals are equal, and O is the midpoint of both, so they bisect each other. A quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal and bisect each other is a rectangle. (b) OA = OB, so angle OBA = angle OAB = 40 degrees and angle AOB = 180 - 80 = 100 degrees. (c) Angle ABC = 90 degrees, so angle OBC = 90 - 40 = 50 degrees, not 45 degrees; the two angle readings cannot both be right. (d) OB = OC, so angle OCB = 45 degrees and angle BOC = 180 - 90 = 90 degrees; then angle AOB = 180 - 90 = 90 degrees and angle OAB = (180 - 90) / 2 = 45 degrees. (e) Angle AOD = 80 degrees gives angle AOB = 180 - 80 = 100 degrees, which matches (b), where angle OAB = 40 degrees. So the 40 degree reading is right and the 45 degree reading of angle OBC was wrong; it should be 50 degrees.
s: Part (a): equal diagonals (18 cm) that bisect each other, so a rectangle
Part (b): angle OBA = 40 and angle AOB = 100 degrees
Part (c): angle OBC must be 50 degrees, so 45 cannot be right
Part (d): angle AOB = 90 and angle OAB = 45 degrees
Part (e): angle AOB = 100 matches the 40 degree reading, so the 45 degree reading was wrong

questions.q:
In rectangle ABCD the diagonals meet at O. Diagonal AC makes with side AD an angle twice the angle it makes with side AB (angle OAD = 2 x angle OAB). Diagonal BD is 14 cm long.
(a) Find angle OAB and angle OAD.
(b) Find angle AOB and angle AOD.
(c) Show that triangle AOD is equilateral.
(d) Find the lengths of AD and BC.
(e) Explain why, in this rectangle, side AD is exactly half of a diagonal.
questions.a: (a) Angle OAB + angle OAD = 90, so 3 x angle OAB = 90: angle OAB = 30 degrees, angle OAD = 60 degrees. (b) OA = OB, so angle OBA = 30 and angle AOB = 180 - 60 = 120 degrees; angle AOD = 180 - 120 = 60 degrees. (c) OA = OD, so angle ODA = angle OAD = 60 degrees; all three angles of triangle AOD are 60 degrees, so it is equilateral. (d) OD = 14 / 2 = 7 cm, so AD = 7 cm, and BC = AD = 7 cm (opposite sides of a rectangle). (e) AD equals OD, and OD is half of BD because the diagonals bisect each other.
s: Part (a): 30 and 60 degrees
Part (b): 120 and 60 degrees
Part (c): all angles of triangle AOD are 60 degrees
Part (d): AD = BC = 7 cm
Part (e): links AD = OD with the diagonals bisecting each other

questions.q:
A workshop in Saharanpur makes wooden photo frames. For each frame the checker measures the two diagonals and where they cross.
Frame A: diagonals 50 cm and 50 cm, crossing at the midpoint of both, one angle between them 74 degrees.
Frame B: diagonals 50 cm and 48 cm, crossing at the midpoint of both.
Frame C: diagonals 50 cm and 50 cm, crossing 20 cm from one end of the first diagonal and at the midpoint of the second.
Frame D: diagonals 46 cm and 46 cm, crossing at the midpoint of both at 90 degrees.
(a) Which frames are certainly rectangles?
(b) Give the reason frame B is not a rectangle.
(c) In frame A, find the angle a diagonal makes with the side opposite the 74 degree angle.
(d) A customer orders frames that are rectangles but not squares. Which frames can be sent? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Frames A and D: their diagonals are equal and bisect each other. (b) The diagonals of a rectangle are always equal; 50 cm and 48 cm are not. (c) The triangle on that side has two 25 cm sides and apex 74 degrees, so the angle is (180 - 74) / 2 = 53 degrees. (d) Only frame A. Frame D's diagonals are equal, bisect each other and meet at 90 degrees, which makes it a square; frames B and C are not rectangles.
s: Part (a): A and D, with the equal-and-bisecting test
Part (b): a rectangle's diagonals must be equal
Part (c): 53 degrees from the isosceles triangle
Part (d): sends only frame A, ruling out D as a square

questions.q:
ABCD is a square floor tile whose diagonals meet at O. Measured from O, the distances to corners A, B and C add up to 21 cm.
(a) Find the length of diagonal BD, naming the properties you use.
(b) Without measuring, find angle AOB, naming the pair of congruent triangles you use.
questions.a: (a) The diagonals of a square are equal and bisect each other, so OA = OB = OC. Each is 21 / 3 = 7 cm, and BD = 2 x 7 = 14 cm. (b) Triangles AOB and COB are congruent by SSS (OA = OC, AB = CB, OB common), so angle AOB = angle COB. Together they make a straight angle, so angle AOB = 90 degrees.
s: Part (a): OA = OB = OC = 7 cm from equal, bisecting diagonals, so BD = 14 cm
Part (b): SSS congruence of triangles AOB and COB and the straight angle, giving 90 degrees

questions.q: True or False: A quadrilateral whose two diagonals are equal and cross at 90 degrees must be a square. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. The diagonals must also bisect each other. For example, two 10 cm sticks crossing at 90 degrees, one at its midpoint (5 cm and 5 cm) and the other at its 3 cm mark (3 cm and 7 cm), have equal, perpendicular diagonals, but the four triangles at the crossing are not all congruent, so the sides are not all equal; the shape is a kite, not a square.

Explains that the diagonals must also bisect each other, with a crossing away from a midpoint as the counter-example

questions.q: Meena says, 'The diagonals of a square bisect its angles. So any quadrilateral whose diagonals bisect its angles must be a square.' Do you agree? Give a reason and an example.
questions.a: No. The first sentence is true, but it does not work backwards. The diagonals of a rhombus also bisect its angles. For example, a rhombus with angles 50, 130, 50 and 130 degrees: each diagonal cuts the 50 degree angles into 25 + 25 and the 130 degree angles into 65 + 65, yet it has no right angle, so it is not a square.
s: Gives the verdict that Meena's conclusion is wrong
Names the rhombus as a quadrilateral whose diagonals also bisect its angles
Gives a definite non-square example with its angles

questions.a: (a) The diagonal bisects the 90 degree angle at P, so angle QPR = 45 degrees and angle QPT = 45 - 15 = 30 degrees. (b) In triangle PQT, angle Q = 90 degrees, so angle PTQ = 180 - 90 - 30 = 60 degrees. (c) Angles PTQ and PTR form a straight angle on QR, so angle PTR = 180 - 60 = 120 degrees.
s: Part (a): 30 degrees using the 45 degree half-angle
Part (b): 60 degrees from triangle PQT
Part (c): 120 degrees from the straight angle

questions.q: Arun says he drew a quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal, bisect each other and cross at 90 degrees, and that two of its sides measure 5 cm and 7 cm. Show that this is impossible.
questions.a: Let the quadrilateral be ABCD with diagonals meeting at O. Since the diagonals are equal and bisect each other, OA = OB = OC = OD. The four triangles AOB, BOC, COD and DOA each have two of these equal sides with a 90 degree angle between them, so they are congruent by SAS. Therefore AB = BC = CD = DA, and all four sides are equal. Sides of 5 cm and 7 cm cannot both occur.
s: Notes that the four half-diagonals are equal
Shows the four triangles at O are congruent by SAS
Concludes all sides are equal, contradicting 5 cm and 7 cm

questions.q:
CASE is a square of side 12 cm.
(a) U, V, W, X are the midpoints of sides CA, AS, SE, EC. Show that the four corner triangles (such as CUX) are congruent.
(b) Deduce that UVWX has four equal sides.
(c) Find the angles of each corner triangle.
(d) Show that every angle of UVWX is 90 degrees and name UVWX.
(e) Now take points P, Q, R, T on CA, AS, SE, EC with CP = AQ = SR = ET = 4 cm. Show that PQRT is also a square.
questions.a: (a) Each corner triangle has two 6 cm sides with the 90 degree corner between them, so they are congruent by SAS. (b) Their third sides UV, VW, WX, XU are corresponding parts, so they are equal. (c) Each is isosceles with a right angle: 90, 45 and 45 degrees. (d) At U, the two 45 degree angles and angle XUV make a straight angle, so angle XUV = 90 degrees; the same holds at V, W and X. All sides equal and all angles 90 degrees: UVWX is a square. (e) Each corner triangle now has legs 4 cm and 8 cm with a right angle between them, so all four are congruent by SAS and PQ = QR = RT = TP. At P the two triangles meet with angles that are the two different acute angles of the same right triangle, which add to 90 degrees, so angle TPQ = 180 - 90 = 90 degrees; similarly at Q, R and T. So PQRT is a square.
s: Part (a): SAS congruence of the corner triangles
Part (b): equal sides of UVWX as corresponding parts
Part (c): 90, 45, 45 degrees
Part (d): 90 degree angles from the straight angle, named a square
Part (e): congruent 4-8 right triangles, acute angles adding to 90, so PQRT is a square

questions.q:
A carpenter asks three apprentices to make a square frame by running a thread round the ends of two strips, AC and BD, crossing at O. Each makes one mistake.
Worker P: two 40 cm strips joined at their midpoints, but at 70 degrees.
Worker Q: two 40 cm strips crossing at 90 degrees, at the midpoint of BD but at the 15 cm mark of AC (OA = 15 cm, OC = 25 cm).
Worker R: a 40 cm strip AC and a 32 cm strip BD, joined at their midpoints at 90 degrees.
(a) For P, find the two angles each strip makes with the sides at a corner, and name P's shape.
(b) For Q, show that triangles AOB and AOD are congruent, and say what this tells you about angle A.
(c) For Q, show that angle A is not 90 degrees.
(d) For R, show that all four sides are equal, and explain why it is still not a square.
(e) For each worker, state the one change that turns the frame into a square.
questions.a: (a) The half-strips are all 20 cm, so the triangles at O are isosceles. With apex 70 degrees the base angles are (180 - 70) / 2 = 55 degrees, and with apex 110 degrees they are (180 - 110) / 2 = 35 degrees; each strip makes 55 degrees with one side and 35 degrees with the other. The corners are 55 + 35 = 90 degrees, so P is a rectangle that is not a square. (b) OB = OD = 20 cm, OA is common and angle AOB = angle AOD = 90 degrees, so the triangles are congruent by SAS. So angle OAB = angle OAD: AC cuts angle A into two equal parts. (c) In triangle AOB, OA = 15 cm and OB = 20 cm are unequal, so it is not isosceles and angle OAB is not equal to angle OBA. Since angle AOB = 90 degrees, angle OAB + angle OBA = 90 degrees, so angle OAB is not 45 degrees, and angle A = 2 x angle OAB is not 90 degrees. (d) The four triangles at O each have two half-strips of 20 cm and 16 cm with a right angle between them, so they are congruent by SAS and all four sides are equal. But the diagonals of a square are equal, and here they are 40 cm and 32 cm, so R is a rhombus that is not a square. (e) P: turn the strips to cross at 90 degrees. Q: move the crossing to the 20 cm mark (midpoint) of AC. R: replace the 32 cm strip with a 40 cm strip.
s: Part (a): 55 and 35 degrees, and P is a rectangle, not a square
Part (b): SAS congruence of AOB and AOD, so AC bisects angle A
Part (c): OA and OB unequal, so angle OAB is not 45 and angle A is not 90 degrees

A tile shop in Jaipur lists its four-sided tiles by their diagonals.

Tile L: diagonals 20 cm and 20 cm, crossing at the midpoint of both at 60 degrees.
Tile M: diagonals 20 cm and 16 cm, crossing at the midpoint of both at 90 degrees.
Tile N: diagonals 20 cm and 20 cm at 90 degrees, crossing 8 cm from one end of the first diagonal and at the midpoint of the second.

(b) Explain why tile N is not even a rectangle.
(c) Find the two angles that a diagonal of tile L makes with the sides at a corner.
(d) The shop says tile M has four equal sides. Is it a square? Justify.

(b) The diagonals of a rectangle bisect each other; tile N's first diagonal is cut into 8 cm and 12 cm. (c) The triangles at the crossing are isosceles with apex 60 degrees (base angles 60 degrees) and apex 120 degrees (base angles 30 degrees), so a diagonal makes 60 degrees with one side and 30 degrees with the other. (d) Not a square. Its four sides are equal (the four triangles at the crossing are congruent by SAS), but a square's diagonals are equal and tile M's are 20 cm and 16 cm, so it is a rhombus that is not a square.

Part (b): diagonals of a rectangle must bisect each other

A line from A at 45 degrees to AB is the diagonal AC (the diagonals of a square bisect its angles), so E must be corner C and the new path is the other diagonal; this fits, as the diagonals of a square cross at 90 degrees.

Part (b): 110 degrees using the 45 degree half-angle

questions.q: Quadrilateral ABCD is dented: corner C is pushed in towards A, so the figure looks like an arrowhead with its tip at A. The angle inside the figure at C is more than 180 degrees, and diagonal AC lies inside the figure while diagonal BD lies outside it. Ali says, 'The angles add up to 360 degrees only for ordinary quadrilaterals like rectangles; this dented one must have a different total.' Is Ali right? Justify, using a diagonal.

Angle A is made of angles BAC and CAD, and the inside angle at C is made of angles BCA and ACD, while angles B and D each belong to one triangle. So the four angles of ABCD are exactly the six angles of the two triangles, and they add to 180 + 180 = 360 degrees, as for any quadrilateral.

Shows the six triangle angles make up the four angles, giving 180 + 180 = 360 degrees

questions.q:

(b) Find the four angles.
(c) Is any pair of opposite sides of ABCD parallel? Check using the angles.
questions.a: (a) For example: angle A is a right angle, angle B is twice angle C, and angle D is 30 degrees more than angle C. (b) 4x + 120 = 360, so x = 60: angle A = 90, angle B = 120, angle C = 60 and angle D = 90 degrees. (c) Yes, exactly one pair. Angle B + angle C = 120 + 60 = 180 degrees, so with BC as a transversal, AB is parallel to DC (also angle D + angle A = 180). But angle A + angle B = 210 degrees, so AD is not parallel to BC.
s: Part (a): angle facts that match each term of the equation
Part (b): x = 60 and the angles 90, 120, 60, 90 degrees
Part (c): AB parallel to DC from 120 + 60 = 180, and AD not parallel to BC

questions.q:
A surveyor in Nashik measures all four corners of four plots, each a quadrilateral ABCD, with the corners in order.
Plot 1: 88, 92, 95, 85 degrees.
Plot 2: 110, 70, 115, 75 degrees.
Plot 3: 100, 80, 100, 80 degrees.
Plot 4: 110, 80, 105, 70 degrees.
(a) Which records cannot be correct?
(b) In plot 2 only angle D was misread. What is the true angle D?
(c) Show that plot 3 has both pairs of opposite sides parallel.
(d) Plot 4 has fences AB and DC that are known to be parallel, and only one corner was misread. Which corners can the surveyor trust, which must he measure again, and what could the true angles be?
questions.a: (a) Plots 2 and 4: their angles add to 370 and 365 degrees, not 360. (b) 360 - (110 + 70 + 115) = 360 - 295 = 65 degrees. (c) Angle A + angle B = 100 + 80 = 180 degrees, so with AB as a transversal AD is parallel to BC; angle B + angle C = 80 + 100 = 180 degrees, so with BC as a transversal AB is parallel to DC. (d) With AB parallel to DC, angle A + angle D and angle B + angle C must each be 180 degrees. A + D = 110 + 70 = 180, so A and D fit and can be trusted; B + C = 80 + 105 = 185, so B or C was misread and both must be measured again. Either B = 180 - 105 = 75 degrees (angles 110, 75, 105, 70) or C = 180 - 80 = 100 degrees (angles 110, 80, 100, 70); both sets add to 360 degrees, so the data alone cannot decide which.
s: Part (a): plots 2 and 4, by adding the angles
Part (b): 65 degrees
Part (c): both pairs of adjacent sums are 180, so both pairs of opposite sides are parallel
Part (d): trusts A and D, re-measures B and C, and gives both possible sets

questions.q:
(a) Meera proves the angle sum of quadrilateral SOME by drawing diagonal SM. She writes: 'Triangle SEM has angles adding to 180 degrees and triangle SOM has angles adding to 180 degrees, so the angles of SOME add up to 360 degrees.' Her teacher says one step is missing. Write the missing step.
In quadrilateral ABCD, AB is parallel to DC. Angle A is 30 degrees more than angle D, and angle C is twice angle B.
(b) Find angles A and D.
(c) Find angles B and C.
(d) Diagonal AC is drawn with angle CAD = 40 degrees. Find angle ACD in two ways, from triangle ACD and from the parallel sides, and show that the two answers agree.
(e) Show that AD is not parallel to BC.
questions.a: (a) She must say how the six triangle angles make the four angles of SOME: the diagonal SM splits angle S into angle ESM + angle MSO and angle M into angle EMS + angle SMO, while angles E and O are whole angles of the triangles. So the six angles together are exactly angles S, O, M and E, and their sum is 180 + 180 = 360 degrees. (b) AB is parallel to DC, so angle A + angle D = 180 degrees (AD is a transversal). With A = D + 30: 2D + 30 = 180, so angle D = 75 and angle A = 105 degrees. (c) Angle B + angle C = 180 degrees (BC is a transversal), and C = 2B, so 3B = 180: angle B = 60 and angle C = 120 degrees. (d) From triangle ACD: angle ACD = 180 - 75 - 40 = 65 degrees. From the parallel sides: angle BAC = 105 - 40 = 65 degrees, and angle ACD = angle BAC as alternate angles (AB parallel to DC, AC a transversal), so angle ACD = 65 degrees. The two agree. (e) Angle A + angle B = 105 + 60 = 165 degrees, not 180, so with AB as a transversal, AD and BC are not parallel.
s: Part (a): the diagonal splits angles S and M, so the six angles are exactly the four angles
Part (b): angle D = 75 and angle A = 105 degrees
Part (c): angle B = 60 and angle C = 120 degrees
Part (d): 65 degrees from the triangle and 65 degrees by alternate angles
Part (e): 105 + 60 = 165, not 180, so AD is not parallel to BC

(d) In triangle PRS, angle PRS = 180 - 60 - 50 = 70 degrees; angle QPR = 120 - 50 = 70 degrees. (e) In triangle PQR, angle PRQ = 180 - 70 - 90 = 20 degrees, and angle R = 70 + 20 = 90 degrees, as given.
s: Part (a): angle S = 60 degrees
Part (b): P = 120 and Q = 90 degrees

Design Y: angle C is twice angle B.

(a) Find angles B, C and D in design X.
(b) Find angles B, C and D in design Y.
(c) Decide which design the school should use, and check that its angles add to 360 degrees.

(c) Both designs give the bench enough room (110 and 135 degrees are both at least 100 degrees), and design Y gives it more. But design Y's corners B and D are only 67.5 degrees, less than the 70 degrees each lamp post needs, while design X gives 80 degrees. So the school should use design X. Check: 90 + 80 + 110 + 80 = 360 degrees.
s: Part (a): B = D = 80 and C = 110 degrees
Part (b): B = D = 67.5 and C = 135 degrees
Part (c): both meet the bench need, only X meets the lamp-post need, so X; with the 360 degree check

questions.q:
A shop in Pune has a folding steel gate made of strips that form parallelograms. In one parallelogram ABCD the sides are AB = 30 cm and BC = 20 cm. When the gate is half open, angle A is 60 degrees and the two diagonals, measured to the nearest 0.1 cm, are BD = 26.5 cm and AC = 43.6 cm. A rivet holds the strips where the diagonals cross, at O.
(a) Find the other three angles of ABCD.
(b) Find OA and OB.
(c) As the gate opens further, at what angle A do the two diagonals become equal, and what shape is ABCD then?
(d) Rahul says, 'However far the gate is opened, the rivet O is always the same distance from A as from C, but it is never the same distance from all four corners.' Judge each half of his claim.
questions.a: (a) Adjacent angles add to 180 degrees and opposite angles are equal: angle B = 120, angle C = 60, angle D = 120 degrees. (b) The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other: OA = 43.6 / 2 = 21.8 cm and OB = 26.5 / 2 = 13.25 cm. (c) When angle A = 90 degrees; then all angles are 90 degrees and ABCD is a rectangle, whose diagonals are equal. (d) Rahul is partly right. The first half is true: the diagonals of every parallelogram bisect each other, so OA = OC (and OB = OD) in every position. The second half is wrong: at 60 degrees O is 21.8 cm from A and C but only 13.25 cm from B and D, yet when angle A reaches 90 degrees the diagonals are equal, so O is then the same distance from all four corners.
s: Part (a): 120, 60, 120 degrees
Part (b): OA = 21.8 cm and OB = 13.25 cm
Part (c): at 90 degrees, a rectangle
Part (d): partly right; OA = OC always, but at 90 degrees (a rectangle) O is equidistant from all four corners

(b) Angle A = 35 + 40 = 75 degrees, so angle B = 180 - 75 = 105 degrees. (c) Triangle ABC is congruent to triangle CDA by ASA: angle BAC = angle DCA (35 degrees), AC is common, and angle BCA = angle DAC (40 degrees). So CD = AB = 8 cm.

Part (b): angle B = 105 degrees

questions.q: Pooja says, 'In a parallelogram, the diagonals bisect each other and they also bisect the angles of the parallelogram.' Which part of her statement is correct? Justify both parts.
questions.a: Only the first part. The diagonals of every parallelogram bisect each other (the triangles on opposite sides of the crossing are congruent by ASA). They do not bisect the angles in general: in a parallelogram with sides 4 cm and 5 cm, the diagonal from a 30 degree corner does not cut it into two 15 degree angles: if diagonal AC bisected angle A, then angle CAB = angle CAD = angle ACB (alternate angles), so triangle ABC would be isosceles with BA = BC, which fails when the sides are 4 cm and 5 cm. Diagonals bisect the angles only in special parallelograms such as the rhombus and square.
s: Gives the verdict: partly right, first part only
Justifies that the diagonals bisect each other
Explains that angle bisection holds only for special cases like the rhombus

questions.q:
LAMP is a parallelogram (sides LA, AM, MP, PL) whose diagonals LM and AP meet at O. A straight rod is fixed through O; it meets side LA at X and side MP at Y.
(a) Show that triangles OXL and OYM are congruent, naming the condition and the facts you use.
(b) Deduce that O is the midpoint of the rod XY.
(c) Deduce that LX = MY.
(d) If LA = 15 cm and LX = 6 cm, find YP.
(e) A student says, 'So any rod through O cuts LA and MP at their midpoints.' Judge this using (d).
questions.a: (a) OL = OM, because the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other. LA is parallel to MP and LM is a transversal, so angle OLX = angle OMY (alternate angles). Angle LOX = angle MOY (vertically opposite angles). So triangles OXL and OYM are congruent by ASA. (b) Corresponding parts give OX = OY, so O is the midpoint of XY. (c) Corresponding parts also give LX = MY. (d) MP = LA = 15 cm (opposite sides) and MY = LX = 6 cm, so YP = 15 - 6 = 9 cm. (e) The student is wrong. In (d) the rod passes through O but X is 6 cm from L, while the midpoint of LA is 7.5 cm from L. What is always true is LX = MY, not that X and Y are midpoints.
s: Part (a): OL = OM, alternate angles and vertically opposite angles, so ASA
Part (b): OX = OY
Part (c): LX = MY
Part (d): YP = 9 cm
Part (e): rejects the claim, since LX = 6 cm is not half of 15 cm

questions.q:
In parallelogram ABCD, angle B = 110 degrees. The bisector of angle A meets side DC at E.
(a) Find angles A, C and D.
(b) Find angle DAE and angle AED, naming the property used.
(c) Find angle AEC.
(d) The bisector of angle B meets the bisector of angle A at G. Find angle AGB.
(e) Show that the answer to (d) is the same for every parallelogram.
questions.a: (a) Angle A = 180 - 110 = 70 degrees, angle C = 70 degrees and angle D = 110 degrees. (b) Angle DAE = 70 / 2 = 35 degrees. AB is parallel to DC with transversal AE, so angle AED = angle EAB = 35 degrees (alternate angles). (c) Angle AEC = 180 - 35 = 145 degrees (linear pair). (d) In triangle AGB, angle GAB = 35 and angle GBA = 55 degrees, so angle AGB = 180 - 90 = 90 degrees. (e) Angle A + angle B = 180 always, so half of each adds to 90, and angle AGB = 180 - 90 = 90 degrees in every parallelogram.
s: Part (a): 70, 70, 110 degrees
Part (b): 35 and 35 degrees with alternate angles
Part (c): 145 degrees
Part (d): 90 degrees
Part (e): half of a 180 degree pair is 90 in every parallelogram

questions.q:
A stage-set maker in Kolkata has three wooden frames, each a quadrilateral ABCD.
Frame P: sides in order 60, 40, 60, 40 cm; angles in order 75, 105, 75, 105 degrees.
Frame Q: sides in order 60, 40, 60, 40 cm; angles all 90 degrees.
Frame R: angles in order A = 80, B = 100, C = 85, D = 95 degrees (sides not measured).
(a) Which frames are parallelograms, and which of them is also a rectangle?
(b) Use the angles of frame R to find which pair of its sides is parallel, and explain why R is not a parallelogram.
(c) The designer needs a leaning frame (no right angles) in which both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, so that panels can slide along either pair. Decide which frame to use and justify.
questions.a: (a) P and Q: in each, the adjacent angles add to 180 degrees, so both pairs of opposite sides are parallel. Q, with all angles 90 degrees, is also a rectangle. (b) Angle A + angle B = 180, so with AB as transversal AD is parallel to BC. But angle B + angle C = 185, not 180, so AB is not parallel to DC; only one pair is parallel, so R is a trapezium, not a parallelogram. (c) Frame P: it is a parallelogram with no right angle. Q has right angles, and R has only one pair of parallel sides.
s: Part (a): P and Q are parallelograms, Q is a rectangle
Part (b): AD parallel to BC from 80 + 100 = 180, and 100 + 85 = 185 rules out a parallelogram
Part (c): chooses P, ruling out Q and R

(a) Show that ABCD is a rhombus.
(b) His helper reports that the two diagonals are 1 m each and cross at 70 degrees. Explain why this report cannot be right.
questions.a: (a) The opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal, so CD = AB = 70 cm and DA = BC = 70 cm. All four sides are equal, so ABCD is a rhombus. (b) The diagonals of a rhombus always cross at 90 degrees, so they cannot cross at 70 degrees. (Also, equal diagonals that bisect each other would make it a rectangle, and a rhombus that is a rectangle is a square, whose diagonals again cross at 90 degrees.)

questions.q: Sunita says, 'Any quadrilateral whose diagonals are perpendicular to each other must be a rhombus.' Do you agree? Give a counter-example if you disagree, and say what extra condition would make her statement correct.
questions.a: No. A kite's diagonals are perpendicular, but a kite need not be a rhombus: for example, a kite with sides 5, 5, 8, 8 cm (AB = BC = 5 cm, CD = DA = 8 cm) has perpendicular diagonals but unequal sides. If the perpendicular diagonals also bisect each other, the four triangles at the crossing are congruent (SAS) and all sides are equal, so it is a rhombus.
s: Gives the verdict: disagrees
Gives a kite with unequal sides as a counter-example

questions.q: Prakash says that in his rhombus PQRS, diagonal PR makes an angle of 35 degrees with side PQ and an angle of 40 degrees with side PS. Show that this cannot be right, and find what angle P would be if the 35 degree measurement is correct.
questions.a: In a rhombus, triangles PQR and PSR are congruent by SSS (PQ = PS, QR = SR, PR common), so angle QPR = angle SPR: a diagonal of a rhombus bisects the angle at each end. The two parts at P would have to be equal, but 35 and 40 degrees are not. If the 35 degree part is correct, angle P = 2 x 35 = 70 degrees.
s: States that the diagonal bisects the angle (with the SSS reason)
Points out 35 and 40 degrees cannot both be right
Finds angle P = 70 degrees

questions.q:
ABCD is a rhombus whose diagonals AC and BD meet at O.
(a) Show that triangles AOB and COB are congruent, naming the condition and the rhombus properties you use.
(b) Deduce that BD is perpendicular to AC.
(c) Rohan says the same proof shows that the diagonals of every parallelogram are perpendicular. Which step fails for a parallelogram that is not a rhombus, and why?
questions.a: (a) AB = CB (all sides of a rhombus are equal), AO = CO (the diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other) and BO is common, so triangle AOB is congruent to triangle COB by SSS. (b) So angle AOB = angle COB. These two angles make a straight angle, so each is 90 degrees, and BD is perpendicular to AC. (c) Step (a) fails: it uses AB = CB, two sides next to each other. In a parallelogram only opposite sides need be equal; with AB = 6 cm and BC = 9 cm, say, the triangles are not congruent, so the right angle does not follow.
s: Part (a): SSS with AB = CB, AO = CO and BO common
Part (b): equal angles on a straight line, so 90 degrees
Part (c): the step AB = CB fails, since adjacent sides of a parallelogram need not be equal

(a) Write the question this working answers: which angle was given as 35 degrees?
(b) Name the rhombus property used in each line.
(c) Find angle ADB by a different route from Rani's.
questions.a: (a) The question gave angle OBA (the angle diagonal BD makes with side AB) as 35 degrees and asked for angles BAD and ABC. (b) Line 1: the diagonals of a rhombus meet at 90 degrees (with the angle sum of triangle AOB). Line 2: a diagonal of a rhombus bisects the angles at its ends. Line 3: adjacent angles of a rhombus add up to 180 degrees. (c) In triangle ABD, AB = AD (sides of a rhombus), so angle ADB = angle ABD = 35 degrees. (Or: angle ADC = angle ABC = 70 degrees and BD bisects it.)
s: Part (a): angle OBA = 35 degrees was given
Part (b): the right angle at O, the bisected angle, and adjacent angles adding to 180
Part (c): angle ADB = 35 degrees by another route, such as the isosceles triangle ABD

questions.q:
ABCD is a rhombus with angle BAD = 70 degrees; its diagonals meet at O. A point P lies on diagonal AC between A and O, and P is joined to B and to D so that angle ABP = 20 degrees.
(a) Show that triangles ABP and ADP are congruent, naming the condition and the rhombus property you use.
(b) Deduce that PB = PD, and find angle ADP.
(c) Find angle APB.
(d) Find angle BPD, the angle at P on the side facing C.
(e) Show that triangles BPO and DPO are congruent, and hence give a new reason why AC is perpendicular to BD.
questions.a: (a) AB = AD (sides of a rhombus), AP is common, and angle BAP = angle DAP = 70 / 2 = 35 degrees, because a diagonal of a rhombus bisects the angles at its ends. So the triangles are congruent by SAS. (b) Corresponding parts give PB = PD and angle ADP = angle ABP = 20 degrees. (c) In triangle ABP, angle APB = 180 - 35 - 20 = 125 degrees. (d) Angle BPC = 180 - 125 = 55 degrees (linear pair on AC); in the same way angle DPC = 55 degrees, so angle BPD = 55 + 55 = 110 degrees. (e) PB = PD, angle BPO = angle DPO = 55 degrees, and PO is common, so the triangles are congruent by SAS. So angle POB = angle POD; they make a straight angle on BD, so each is 90 degrees, and AC is perpendicular to BD.
s: Part (a): SAS with AB = AD, AP common and the bisected 35 degree angles
Part (b): PB = PD and angle ADP = 20 degrees
Part (c): angle APB = 125 degrees
Part (d): angle BPD = 110 degrees
Part (e): SAS on BPO and DPO, so equal angles on a straight line are 90 degrees

questions.q:
Two cardboard copies of an isosceles triangle with sides 10 cm, 10 cm and 7 cm are joined along a pair of equal sides.
(a) They are joined along their 7 cm sides. Name the quadrilateral and justify.
(b) They are joined along a 10 cm side so that one is flipped over that side onto the other side of it. Name the quadrilateral and justify.
(c) They are joined along a 10 cm side with one triangle turned half a turn, so that its 7 cm side is opposite the other's 7 cm side. Name the quadrilateral and justify.
(d) Which of the quadrilaterals in (a) to (c) have perpendicular diagonals?
(e) In the kite of (b), the joining side is one diagonal. What does it do to the other diagonal? Explain.
questions.a: (a) A rhombus: the four outer sides are all 10 cm. (b) A kite: going round, the sides are 10, 7, 7, 10 cm, so two pairs of adjacent sides are equal and not all four are equal. (c) A parallelogram: the sides in order are 10, 7, 10, 7 cm, so the opposite sides are equal, and a quadrilateral with equal opposite sides is a parallelogram (draw a diagonal; the two triangles are congruent by SSS, giving equal alternate angles). (d) The rhombus in (a) and the kite in (b). (e) It bisects the other diagonal (the one joining the two free corners of the triangles) at 90 degrees: in a kite, the diagonal through the two corners where equal sides meet is the perpendicular bisector of the other diagonal (the triangles on either side of the crossing are congruent by SAS).
s: Part (a): rhombus, four 10 cm sides
Part (b): kite, sides 10, 7, 7, 10
Part (c): parallelogram from equal opposite sides
Part (d): the rhombus and the kite
Part (e): it is the perpendicular bisector of the other diagonal

questions.q:
In rhombus ABCD the diagonals meet at O, with angle DAC = (2x + 5) degrees and angle BAC = (3x - 10) degrees.
(a) Find x, naming the property used.
(b) Find angle A and angle B.
(c) Find angle ABD.
(d) AO = (y + 6) cm and OC = (2y - 1) cm. Find y and the length of AC.
(e) Could diagonal BD also be as long as AC? Justify.
questions.a: (a) The diagonals of a rhombus bisect its angles, so 2x + 5 = 3x - 10, giving x = 15 (each part 35 degrees). (b) Angle A = 70 degrees and angle B = 180 - 70 = 110 degrees. (c) Angle ABD = 110 / 2 = 55 degrees. (d) The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other, so y + 6 = 2y - 1, giving y = 7; AO = 13 cm and AC = 26 cm. (e) No. If BD were also 26 cm, the diagonals would be equal and bisect each other, so ABCD would be a rectangle; a rhombus that is a rectangle is a square, with all angles 90 degrees. But angle A = 70 degrees, so BD cannot equal AC.
s: Part (a): x = 15 from the angle-bisecting diagonal
Part (b): 70 and 110 degrees
Part (c): 55 degrees
Part (d): y = 7 and AC = 26 cm from the bisecting diagonals
Part (e): equal diagonals would make it a square, but angle A is 70 degrees

questions.q:
A jaali (stone screen) maker in Ahmedabad prepares quadrilateral openings by crossing two iron bars as diagonals. His order sheet reads:
Design J1: bars 18 cm and 12 cm, crossing at the midpoint of both at 90 degrees; the 18 cm bar makes an angle of 33.7 degrees with each side at its ends.
Design J2: bars 18 cm and 18 cm, crossing at the midpoint of both at 90 degrees.
Design J3: bars 18 cm and 12 cm, crossing at the midpoint of both at 70 degrees.
(a) Which designs give a rhombus?
(b) Name the shape of J3, with a reason.
(c) Find all four angles of J1, and the angle the 12 cm bar makes with each side.
(d) The customer wants openings with no right-angled corner, but whose bars cross at right angles so they can be welded crosswise. Decide which design to make and justify.
questions.a: (a) J1 and J2: their diagonals bisect each other at 90 degrees, so the four triangles at the crossing are congruent (SAS) and all sides are equal. (b) A parallelogram that is not a rhombus: its diagonals bisect each other but are not perpendicular. (c) The 18 cm bar bisects the corners at its ends, so those corners are 2 x 33.7 = 67.4 degrees; the other two corners are 180 - 67.4 = 112.6 degrees. The 12 cm bar makes 90 - 33.7 = 56.3 degrees with each side. (d) J1. J2 is a square (equal diagonals bisecting at 90 degrees), so it has right-angled corners; J3's bars do not cross at 90 degrees.
s: Part (a): J1 and J2
Part (b): parallelogram, diagonals bisect but are not perpendicular
Part (c): 67.4, 112.6 degrees and 56.3 degrees
Part (d): chooses J1, ruling out the square J2 and J3

questions.q:
A paper-craft teacher in Bhopal folds a sheet in half and then in half again, and makes one straight cut across the folded corner at the centre. When the sheet is opened, the two creases cross at 90 degrees at the centre of the sheet, and the hole has its four corners on the creases: 6 cm on either side of the centre along one crease and 4 cm on either side along the other.
(a) Treating the lines joining opposite corners of the hole as its diagonals, give their lengths and say where and at what angle they cross.
(b) Name the shape of the hole and justify.
(c) What cut, measured along each crease from the centre, would give a square hole with diagonals of 10 cm? Justify.
(d) For a lantern, the teacher wants the hole as tall as possible (longest diagonal), but a bulb holder 7 cm wide must pass through it along its shorter diagonal. She can cut 6 cm and 4 cm, or 7 cm and 3 cm. Decide which cut to use and justify.
questions.a: (a) 12 cm and 8 cm; they cross at the centre, which is the midpoint of both, at 90 degrees. (b) A rhombus that is not a square. The diagonals bisect each other at 90 degrees, so the four triangles at the centre (each with arms of 6 cm and 4 cm and a right angle between them) are congruent by SAS and all four sides are equal; the diagonals are unequal, so it is not a square. (c) 5 cm along each crease: the diagonals are then 10 cm and 10 cm, equal and bisecting each other at 90 degrees, which gives a square. (d) The 6 cm and 4 cm cut. The 7 cm and 3 cm cut would be taller (diagonals 14 cm and 6 cm), but its shorter diagonal, 6 cm, is less than the 7 cm the bulb holder needs. The 6 cm and 4 cm cut gives a shorter diagonal of 8 cm, which is enough, so it is the tallest hole that works.
s: Part (a): diagonals 12 cm and 8 cm, bisecting each other at 90 degrees
Part (b): rhombus, by SAS on the four triangles, not a square as the diagonals are unequal
Part (c): 5 cm along each crease, equal diagonals bisecting at 90 degrees
Part (d): chooses 6 cm and 4 cm, since the taller cut's 6 cm diagonal is too narrow

(a) Find angle U.
(b) Find angles V and W, naming the property used.
questions.a: (a) Angles U and X lie between the parallel sides on the same side of UX, so angle U = 180 - 112 = 68 degrees. (b) In an isosceles trapezium the angles at each end of a parallel side are equal, so angle V = angle U = 68 degrees and angle W = angle X = 112 degrees.
s: Part (a): 68 degrees from angles between parallel sides adding to 180
Part (b): V = 68 and W = 112 degrees from the isosceles trapezium property

questions.q: Two cardboard copies of a triangle with sides 5 cm, 8 cm and 11 cm are joined along their 11 cm sides, one flipped over that side so that it lies on the other side of it. Which quadrilateral is formed?
questions.a: A kite with sides 5, 5, 8 and 8 cm
o: A kite with sides 5, 5, 8 and 8 cm
A parallelogram with sides 5, 8, 5, 8 cm
A rhombus with all sides 8 cm
A trapezium with sides 5, 8, 11, 11 cm

questions.a: All four of its corner angles are equal
o: All four of its corner angles are equal
Its two diagonals are equal to each other in length

questions.q:
The same two 5-8-11 cm triangles are now joined along their 8 cm sides, with one triangle turned half a turn so that each 5 cm side lies opposite the other triangle's 5 cm side.
(a) Write the four sides of the quadrilateral in order.
(b) Name the quadrilateral and justify.
questions.a: (a) 11, 5, 11, 5 cm. (b) A parallelogram: both pairs of opposite sides are equal. Drawing the joining side as a diagonal, the two triangles are congruent (SSS), so the alternate angles at its ends are equal and both pairs of opposite sides are parallel.
s: Part (a): sides 11, 5, 11, 5 cm
Part (b): parallelogram, justified by equal opposite sides and alternate angles

questions.q:
Quadrilateral ABCD is a kite (AB = BC and CD = DA) and also a trapezium, with AB parallel to DC.
(a) Show that angle B = angle D.
(b) Hence name the quadrilateral, with a reason.
questions.a: (a) In a kite, angle A = angle C (triangles ABD and CBD are congruent by SSS). AB is parallel to DC, so angle A + angle D = 180 degrees (AD a transversal) and angle B + angle C = 180 degrees (BC a transversal). So angle D = 180 - angle A and angle B = 180 - angle C = 180 - angle A, giving angle B = angle D. (b) A rhombus. Both pairs of opposite angles are equal, so ABCD is a parallelogram and its opposite sides are equal: AB = CD. With AB = BC and CD = DA, all four sides are equal.
s: Part (a): uses angle A = angle C and the two co-interior pairs to get angle B = angle D
Part (b): a parallelogram with AB = BC, so all sides equal: a rhombus

questions.q:
ABCD is a trapezium with AB parallel to DC, and angle A is 3 times angle D.
(a) Find angles A and D.
(b) If angle C = 70 degrees, find angle B.
questions.a: (a) Angle A + angle D = 180 (between the parallel sides, on the same side of AD), so 4 x angle D = 180: angle D = 45 and angle A = 135 degrees. (b) Angle B + angle C = 180, so angle B = 110 degrees.
s: Part (a): D = 45 and A = 135 degrees
Part (b): B = 110 degrees

questions.q: Ravi says, 'In a kite, the two diagonals bisect each other at right angles, just like in a rhombus.' How much of his statement is correct? Explain with kite ABCD, where AB = BC and CD = DA.
questions.a: Partly right. The diagonals of a kite do meet at right angles, and diagonal BD bisects AC (triangles AOB and COB are congruent by SAS, giving AO = OC and right angles at O). But AC does not in general bisect BD: in a kite with AB = BC = 5 cm and CD = DA = 12 cm, B is much nearer the crossing point than D. Only when all four sides are equal (a rhombus) do both diagonals bisect each other.
s: Gives the verdict: partly right
Confirms the right angle and that BD bisects AC
Explains that AC need not bisect BD except in a rhombus

questions.q: Shreya says her isosceles trapezium UVWX, with UV parallel to XW and UX = VW, has angle U = 70 degrees and angle W = 100 degrees. Show that these two measurements cannot both be right.
questions.a: Angles U and X are between the parallel sides on the same side of UX, so angle X = 180 - 70 = 110 degrees. In an isosceles trapezium the angles at each end of a parallel side are equal, so angle W = angle X = 110 degrees. This contradicts 100 degrees. (Equally, angle V = angle U = 70, and angle V + angle W should be 180, but 70 + 100 = 170.)
s: Finds angle X = 110 degrees
Uses the isosceles property: angle W = angle X
States the contradiction with 100 degrees

questions.q:
ABCD is a trapezium with AB parallel to DC. Its angles are angle A = (2x + 10) degrees, angle D = (3x - 40) degrees and angle B = (x + 30) degrees.
(a) Find x, and angles A and D.
(b) Find angles B and C.
(c) Is ABCD an isosceles trapezium? Justify using its angles.
questions.a: (a) AB is parallel to DC, so angle A + angle D = 180 degrees (AD is a transversal): 5x - 30 = 180, so x = 42. Angle A = 94 degrees and angle D = 86 degrees. (b) Angle B = 42 + 30 = 72 degrees, and angle B + angle C = 180, so angle C = 108 degrees. (c) No. In an isosceles trapezium the angles at the two ends of a parallel side are equal, but at the ends of AB they are 94 and 72 degrees (and at the ends of DC, 86 and 108 degrees). So its non-parallel sides AD and BC cannot be equal.
s: Part (a): x = 42, angle A = 94 and angle D = 86 degrees
Part (b): angle B = 72 and angle C = 108 degrees
Part (c): not isosceles, since the angles at the ends of a parallel side differ

questions.q:
For Uttarayan in Ahmedabad, a kite-maker builds a frame ABCD with AB = BC = 25 cm and CD = DA = 44 cm. The spine runs along diagonal BD and a cross-stick along diagonal AC, which measures 37.2 cm. He sets angle ABC = 96 degrees, and angle ADC comes out as 50 degrees.
(a) Find angle BAD.
(b) Find angle ABD and angle BAC.
(c) Where along the cross-stick, and at what angle, must the spine cross it?
(d) To save string he wants the cross-stick to cross the spine at the spine's midpoint as well. Can he keep these side lengths? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Angles A and C are equal, so angle BAD = (360 - 96 - 50) / 2 = 107 degrees. (b) The spine BD bisects angle B, so angle ABD = 48 degrees; the diagonals are perpendicular, so angle BAC = 180 - 90 - 48 = 42 degrees. (c) At the middle of the cross-stick, 37.2 / 2 = 18.6 cm from A, and at 90 degrees, since BD is the perpendicular bisector of AC. (d) No. If each diagonal bisected the other, the frame would be a parallelogram; a parallelogram with AB = BC has all four sides equal (a rhombus). But AB = 25 cm and DA = 44 cm, so the spine's midpoint cannot be the crossing point.
s: Part (a): 107 degrees
Part (b): 48 and 42 degrees
Part (c): 18.6 cm from A, at 90 degrees
Part (d): no, since bisecting diagonals with AB = BC would force a rhombus

questions.q:
Tanvi writes this proof for kite ABCD (AB = BC, CD = DA) whose diagonals meet at O:
Step 1: In triangles AOB and COB, AB = CB, angle ABO = angle CBO, and BO is common, so they are congruent by SAS.
Step 2: So AO = CO, and angle AOB = angle COB = 90 degrees, as they make a straight angle.
(a) Which fact in Step 1 has Tanvi used without proving it?
(b) Prove that fact, naming the triangles and the congruence condition.
(c) With your step added first, is the proof complete, or does it go round in a circle? Explain.
(d) Tanvi's friend tries the same steps with triangles BOA and DOA to prove BO = DO. Which step breaks, and why?
(e) In kite PQRS (PQ = QR, RS = SP) the diagonals meet at T, angle QPR = 38 degrees and angle RPS = 52 degrees. Find angle PQS and angle QRS.
questions.a: (a) That angle ABO = angle CBO, that is, that diagonal BD bisects angle B. (b) In triangles ABD and CBD, AB = CB, AD = CD and BD is common, so they are congruent by SSS, and angle ABD = angle CBD. (c) It is complete and not circular: the new step uses only the given sides, and Steps 1 and 2 then use its result, not the result they are proving. (d) Step 1 breaks: it would need AB = AD, two sides that meet at A, but in a kite AB = BC and AD = DC, so AB need not equal AD; the triangles need not be congruent, and AC need not bisect BD. (e) Diagonal QS is perpendicular to PR, so in triangle PQT, angle PQT = 180 - 90 - 38 = 52 degrees; so angle PQS = 52 degrees. Angle QRS = angle QPS (the kite's equal pair of angles) = 38 + 52 = 90 degrees.
s: Part (a): angle ABO = angle CBO was not proved
Part (b): SSS congruence of triangles ABD and CBD
Part (c): complete, not circular, as the new step uses only the given sides
Part (d): the step fails because AB need not equal AD
Part (e): angle PQS = 52 and angle QRS = 90 degrees

questions.q:
A building inspector's checklist has five statements about quadrilaterals. Say whether each is true or false, with a one-line justification.
(a) A quadrilateral whose diagonals bisect each other at 90 degrees must be a square.
(b) If both pairs of opposite angles of a quadrilateral are equal, both pairs of opposite sides are parallel.
(c) An isosceles trapezium can have four different angles.
(d) A kite in which all four angles are equal must be a square.
(e) A quadrilateral with two right angles at the ends of one side has a pair of parallel sides.
questions.a: (a) False: such diagonals give a rhombus; it is a square only if the diagonals are also equal. (b) True: if angle A = angle C and angle B = angle D, then 2A + 2B = 360, so A + B = 180, which makes AD parallel to BC; similarly A + D = 180 makes AB parallel to DC. (c) False: the angles at each end of a parallel side are equal, so it has at most two different angles. (d) True: equal angles are 90 degrees each, so it is a rectangle; with AB = BC its adjacent sides are equal, so all sides are equal and it is a square. (e) True: if angle A = angle B = 90 degrees, then with AB as a transversal the angles on the same side add to 180 degrees, so AD is parallel to BC and the quadrilateral is a trapezium.
s: Part (a): false, a rhombus
Part (b): true, A + B = 180 gives parallel sides
Part (c): false, angles pair up equally
Part (d): true, a rectangle with equal adjacent sides
Part (e): true, the two right angles add to 180, so the sides are parallel

questions.q:
An irrigation canal in Punjab has a cross-section that is an isosceles trapezium ABCD: the water surface AB is parallel to the bed DC, and the two banks AD and BC are equal. The angle inside the canal between the bed and bank AD is angle D = 118 degrees.
(a) Find angle C.
(b) Find the angles at the top corners A and B.
(c) To reduce erosion, an engineer wants each bank to make an angle of 55 degrees with the water surface. What must the bed angles become?
(d) A contractor proposes a canal with bed angles of 118 degrees at D and 125 degrees at C, the surface still parallel to the bed. Find its top angles, and decide whether its two banks can be equal. Justify.
questions.a: (a) In an isosceles trapezium the angles at each end of a parallel side are equal, so angle C = 118 degrees. (b) Angles A and D are between the parallel sides on the same side of AD, so angle A = 180 - 118 = 62 degrees; likewise angle B = 62 degrees. (c) If angle A = angle B = 55 degrees, then angle D = angle C = 180 - 55 = 125 degrees. (d) Angle A = 180 - 118 = 62 degrees and angle B = 180 - 125 = 55 degrees. The banks cannot be equal: if they were, the trapezium would be isosceles and the angles at the ends of the bed would be equal, but 118 and 125 degrees are not.
s: Part (a): 118 degrees
Part (b): 62 degrees each
Part (c): 125 degrees each
Part (d): top angles 62 and 55 degrees, and the banks cannot be equal
